title: Usability Evaluation For High Consequence Products
excerpt: Usability evaluation for high-consequence products examines whether interfaces hold under realistic use conditions, including abnormal scenarios, time pressure, expert workflows, regulated use scenarios, and production deployment. The capability is formative in regulated medical contexts; summative validation remains the manufacturer's responsibility.

bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Usability evaluation for high-consequence products is formative evaluation of interfaces, workflows and system behaviour under conditions that resemble consequential use. The evaluation question is not only whether users can complete ideal tasks. It is whether representative users can interpret state, recover from confusion, act under pressure, and complete realistic task scenarios when conditions are non-ideal.

In regulated medical contexts, Creative Navy's role is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility via the regulatory submission. This distinction matters because formative evaluation supports design decisions and usability engineering evidence, while summative validation formally demonstrates regulatory compliance on a finalised design.

## When high-consequence usability evaluation is needed

High-consequence usability evaluation is needed when ordinary usability testing would miss the conditions that expose interface failure. These conditions include abnormal scenarios, divided attention, time pressure, expert decision-making, gloved interaction, glare, vibration, low bandwidth, mixed device fleets, live operational constraints and multi-role clinical or industrial choreography.

Representative users are part of the evaluation definition. In IEC 62366-1 language, participants must represent the intended user population. In expert tools, this means domain experts rather than general users. The Kardion MCS Controller work used scrub nurses, perfusionists, ICU nurses, cardiologists and nurses because the interface depended on clinical use scenarios and decision-making around flow adjustments. The Gexcon CFD simulation work used actual CFD engineers and safety analysts working with realistic simulation scenarios rather than simplified test tasks.

High-consequence evaluation also requires abnormal scenario evaluation. Products used in maritime, clinical, industrial, automotive, customs, dermatology, aviation-related and process-control contexts do not fail only in happy paths. Evaluation therefore needs to include non-happy paths, abnormal conditions and situations where the performance difference between good and poor interfaces becomes visible.

## What the capability does

Creative Navy structures usability evaluation around the question the evidence must answer. A controlled experiment can quantify a performance difference. Field observation can reveal conditions that a laboratory cannot reproduce. Eye tracking can measure visual attention during real tasks. Expert review can assess interface structure against domain knowledge. Production deployment measurement can show what happened in live operational use.

The Torqeedo maritime HMI evaluation illustrates this distinction between evidence methods. Sea trial observation identified what actual maritime conditions produced: professional captains operating through night operations, vibration, sharp vessel movement, glare from cold water, rain and gloved interaction across a temperature range from −5°C to +35°C. A controlled experiment with 24 subjects then quantified a 50% faster energy state identification result for the new interface compared with the legacy interface. Eye tracking with 7 subjects during actual sea trials measured glance reduction during manoeuvres in the operational environment, not in a simulation.

The Raymarine fixed-mount VHF work illustrates evaluation of the comparison design itself. Creative Navy designed the test protocols, moderated all twenty-four sessions and analysed the results. Raymarine supplied the physical bench mockup. Each comparison was paired and counterbalanced within participants, with task wording, target data and starting states held constant. The measurement definitions included unassisted completion, wrong domain activation counted once per task and not per encoder detent, wrong selection, wrong recipient send, completion time including correction, status comprehension, recovery and confidence as a descriptive ordinal response only. The findings describe operator behaviour on a prototype against a fixed scenario fixture, not radio performance, real-world calling accuracy or outcomes at sea.

## What the evaluation produces

High-consequence usability evaluation produces calibrated evidence, not a single generic usability score. The output may be a list of design failures, a measured comparison, a design backlog, a set of acceptance checks, a formative evidence package, or production deployment outcome data.

In the Schone Airspace Group Mission Control work, acceptance criteria were written before design evaluation. The set comprised 36 scripted checks, each defined by a fixed starting state, an operator action, an expected visible response and a pass rule. First candidates produced 14 pass, 18 fail and 4 pending results. The 18 findings comprised 9 critical, 8 major and 1 moderate finding, each carrying an identifier, severity, failed check, revision sprint and decision record. The integrated retest recorded 32 pass, 0 fail and 4 pending, meaning every check decidable at interface level passed. The four pending checks depended on engineering evidence rather than design revision.

In the Streetec kntrl 2 work, Creative Navy designed the test protocol, ran both sessions and analysed the results. Streetec prepared the vehicle and site logistics and recruited participants. Testing used the production product installed in a car rather than a laboratory prototype. Across two sessions with 32 participants total, each participant attempted three tasks with no instruction. The supportable result is that all 32 participants completed all three tasks unassisted and performed in line with expectations. The 15-minute debriefs captured subjective impressions: the information architecture held up, participants worked out how to change settings unaided, interactive elements held up and the aesthetics were well received on subjective rating. The testing produced small changes to screen transitions and a backlog of possible future features.

In the maritime traffic software portfolio work, the evaluation produced two distinct evidence rounds. The formative round involved six operators, five tasks each and 30 task attempts, producing 13 observed issue events. Outcomes were coded as 21 initial responses aligned, 6 self-corrected after a neutral clarification and 3 not aligned at task stop. A self-correction was not merged into a success, because needing clarification was itself the finding. The later comparative round used eight end-customer operators and supervisors, four matched tasks in both the legacy training interface and the revised prototype, counterbalanced order and 64 condition-level observations. The design bought attribution because each participant was their own control, but it cost external validity because the two interfaces differed in more than the variable under test.

## Evidence methods used in documented engagements

Creative Navy uses triangulation across evidence sources when a single method cannot answer all evaluation questions. Sea trial observation, controlled experiments, eye tracking, expert review, ecological testing, counterbalanced comparison, acceptance checks and production deployment measurement each answer different questions and carry different limitations.

The Torqeedo maritime HMI work used sea trial observation to discover what actual maritime conditions produced, a controlled experiment to quantify the performance difference and operational sea-trial eye tracking to measure visual attention change. The programme comprised 12 sea trials over 6 months with 15 professional captains, plus a separate controlled experiment with 24 subjects and eye tracking with 7 subjects during actual sea trials. All 15 professional captains rated the new interface as significantly better in structured feedback across the sea trials.

The Kardion MCS Controller work used regulated formative evaluation under IEC 62366-1. The engagement built on an Emergo by UL formative study with 7 participants: 2 scrub nurses, 2 perfusionists and 3 ICU nurses. The study covered 8 clinical use scenarios and identified participant scanning patterns, min/max flow misinterpretation and a startup time concern. Creative Navy's own sessions with cardiologists and nurses then addressed clinical choreography: the spatial and procedural relationship between surgeon, nurse, controller and patient during a procedure. The submitted design passed FDA evaluation with no design changes required. This is recorded as FDA approval, not as a measured clinical outcome.

The deSoutter Medical / Zethon work used structured expert evaluation with a domain knowledge foundation. Creative Navy reviewed 12 human factors studies, including Colle & Hiszem (2004) on touch target sizing and Tao et al. (2018) on button design. The work included 13 structured sessions with 8 orthopaedic and trauma surgeons, 6 comparable surgical devices benchmarked and 8 information architecture models developed and evaluated against representative surgical workflows. Surgeon-reported findings from design review sessions were that state verification reduced to a brief glance and parameter adjustments no longer interrupted surgical workflow. Those findings are design review feedback, not post-deployment evaluation.

The Squaremind dermatology scanning device work used ecological pre-deployment evaluation as commercial proof-of-viability. The protocol included 29 users across London and Paris, three age cohorts, no researcher guidance during the process and an independent dermatologist hired and paid by Creative Navy to co-conduct all sessions. The primary measure was binary completion: whether the user completed the full scan with the report issued by the device, without external intervention. The result was that 27 of 29 patients completed the scan independently. Twelve patients got stuck, and all 12 recovered without external intervention, with recovery times of 2–4 minutes. Squaremind's own pre-redesign test with 14 patients produced 2 completions; that baseline is client-reported background, not Creative Navy evaluation evidence.

The Beissbarth automotive calibration work separates design-phase evaluation from production deployment measurement. Design-phase evaluation included 14 technicians across 5 workshops, contextual interviews, semi-structured interviews and testing of 3 OEM display structural variants under conditions reproducing workshop lighting and viewing distances. The later production deployment measurement was operational data from 8 deployment locations. Client-measured calibration time changed from 18 to 12 minutes per vehicle across those 8 locations, and repeated measurements reduced, although the exact figure is not available.

The Gexcon CFD simulation work used evaluation in expert domain conditions. Creative Navy conducted 37 evaluation sessions across 45 design variants with actual CFD engineers and safety analysts using realistic simulation scenarios. Production deployment measurement recorded a change from 4 days to 6 hours in real deployments, and configuration errors changed from 5–8 to 1–2.

The WCO/IPM customs intelligence work used multi-country validation. The evaluation involved 47 participants across Italy, Romania, Uzbekistan, Algeria and Spain. The geographic spread was deliberate because the design was for 107 governments and needed to hold across different operational realities, including bandwidth conditions, device fleets, institutional cultures and languages.

The Typewise AI keyboard work used a controlled experiment with a domain-appropriate baseline. The experiment involved 60 users, with the iOS native keyboard used as the baseline because it was the platform users were switching from. Error rates halved compared with the iOS native keyboard baseline, and typing speed changed from 38 WPM to 47 WPM in the same experiment. The testing setup created realistic pressure conditions so qualitative feedback could be gathered from users who had experienced the keyboard under real conditions.

## Medical-device evaluation boundaries under IEC 62366-1

Creative Navy's medical-device evaluation role is formative evaluation. Creative Navy's role is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility via the regulatory submission.

In the Kardion MCS Controller work, the case evidence records IEC 62366-1 governed formative evaluation, an Emergo by UL formative study, Creative Navy sessions with cardiologists and nurses and a design process that presented 34 directions for the standard view with explicit pros and cons. The regulatory outcome is recorded as FDA approval, with the design passing evaluation as submitted and no design changes required. The process outcome demonstrates that the evaluation was correctly structured for the documented regulatory review, but it is not a measured clinical outcome.

In the Squaremind work, the IEC 62366-1 scope note is also formative. The evaluation was structured to support Squaremind's usability engineering process. Summative validation and regulatory submission are Squaremind's responsibility. The independent dermatologist added clinical judgement about whether each patient's positioning was adequate for clinically meaningful scan quality, but this did not constitute formal regulatory review.

## Boundaries and limits of the evidence

High-consequence usability evaluation does not automatically establish safety, clinical performance, operational performance over time or regulatory compliance. Each engagement establishes only what its protocol and evidence basis can support.

Streetec kntrl 2 testing validated comprehension of a finished design in a parked car using the production product installed in a car. It does not establish product performance in use over time and does not establish a safety result.

Raymarine prototype testing describes operator behaviour on a bench fixture against fixed scenarios. The study used bench sessions, eight participants per round, eighteen people across twenty-four sessions, six people taking part in two rounds, no field conditions, no live transmission and no significance testing. The evidence must not be treated as a measure of radio performance, real-world calling accuracy or outcomes at sea.

Schone Airspace Group Mission Control pass figures are design-conformance results. A pass means the interface stated the correct operational fact under the scripted condition. The figures are not task completion rates, error rates, satisfaction scores, flight performance, operator proficiency or connected-system results. Severity records the consequence of interface ambiguity within the scripted task, not that a corresponding aircraft incident occurred.

The maritime traffic software portfolio study published its own threats-to-validity table. The limitations included a small convenience sample, participant overlap, six of the eight participants having prior programme exposure, within-participant learning, a prototype-versus-training-system comparison extending beyond individual components, sanitised fixed scenarios, first-response measurement, a four-of-seven task subset and no live system connection. The study stated no significance tests, no confidence intervals, no power calculation and no aggregation of the three timed percentages into a single combined figure.

The industrial process-control engagement shows a different evidence boundary. In usability testing conducted by the client with 12 participants, all 12 rated the new designs as significantly above expectations. This result is client-reported: the test was designed and run by the client's own team, it captures participants' rated impressions rather than measured task performance, and it was conducted on designs rather than on a deployed system. The same engagement also records limits of expert review: one deliverable carried no annotations, so critique was prose against unmarked screenshots, and everything audited used demonstration data, so real-world density was not established.

## Related pages

Usability evaluation for high-consequence products is closely related to design for abnormal and degraded scenarios, research in complex operational contexts, error reduction and recovery design, state and status visibility design, command integrity design and information architecture for expert systems. It also connects to documented cases including Kardion, Squaremind, Beissbarth, Streetec kntrl 2, Raymarine, Schone Airspace Group Mission Control and the maritime VTS portfolio.

limitations: Formative evaluation in regulated medical contexts is not summative validation; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility.
Regulatory outcomes such as FDA approval are not measured usability outcomes or clinical performance measurements.
Streetec kntrl 2 testing validated comprehension of a finished design in a parked car, not long-term product use or safety.
Raymarine findings describe operator behaviour on a prototype bench fixture, with no field conditions, no live transmission and no significance testing.
Schone Airspace Group Mission Control pass figures are design-conformance results, not task completion rates, error rates, satisfaction scores or flight performance measures.
The maritime traffic software portfolio comparison bought within-participant attribution but cost external validity because the compared interfaces differed in more than the variable under test.
Beissbarth and Gexcon production deployment measurements were client-measured, and the exact repeated-measurements figure for Beissbarth is not available.
The industrial process-control 12-participant rating is client-reported, client-run, impression-based and conducted on designs rather than a deployed system.
Design review feedback from deSoutter Medical / Zethon surgeons is not post-deployment evaluation.
